claims.text: The elevated-temperature wear transition in FeNiCrCoCu coatings is driven by a thermally activated reduction in stacking-fault energy.
Reducing stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning.
Reducing stacking-fault energy promotes rapid dislocation multiplication.
Increasing temperature promotes dislocation cross-slip by reducing stacking-fault energy or thermally lowering its activation barrier.
Rapid dislocation multiplication and cross-slip produce localized lattice softening.
Localized lattice softening accelerates wear.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has a single-phase FCC structure.
The coating has stable wear resistance at 300 K.
The coating has a high elastic modulus at 300 K.
The room-temperature coating has a low dislocation density.
Deformation twinning is suppressed at room temperature.
Deformation at approximately 300 K is dominated by dislocation slip.
The critical stress for deformation twinning is approximately 235 MPa.
Dislocation density increases sharply above the critical temperature.
Elevated temperature causes dislocation tangles to form.
Loss of twinning as a hardening mechanism reduces wear resistance.
Increased dislocation mobility accelerates material removal.
Wear resistance declines sharply above approximately 450–500 K.
Elastic modulus declines sharply above approximately 450–500 K.
The microstructure transitions from twinning-dominated deformation below the threshold to slip-dominated deformation above it.

contradictions.description: The initial-state and baseline fields say deformation at 300 K is primarily dislocation slip with minimal or suppressed twinning, whereas the predicted outcome describes the temperature transition as twinning-dominated to slip-dominated. No lower-temperature twinning-dominated regime is defined.

The mechanism attributes declining wear to loss of twinning as a hardening mechanism, but the hypothesis and baseline already characterize twinning as suppressed or limited in the stable room-temperature state.
